alt: Three plan sketches across a boundary between the defendant’s and claimant’s land: encroachment by tree roots and branches; physical damage from fumes damaging crops, where locality is irrelevant (St Helen’s Smelting v Tipping); and interference with comfort and enjoyment from noise, where the balancing factors decide.
caption: Physical damage is a nuisance anywhere; comfort claims depend on balancing.

alt: Claimants need a proprietary interest in the land, as an owner or tenant; in Hunter v Canary Wharf family members without an interest could not sue. Defendants can be the creator of the nuisance, the occupier where they adopt or continue a trespasser’s or natural nuisance (Sedleigh-Denfield; Leakey v National Trust), or a landlord who authorised it.
caption: Only those with an interest in land can sue; creators, occupiers and authorising landlords can be sued.

alt: Factors deciding unreasonableness: locality (Sturges v Bridgman), duration and timing (Halsey v Esso), sensitivity (Robinson v Kilvert, now foreseeability in Network Rail v Morris), malice (Christie v Davey; Hollywood Silver Fox Farm) and new forms (Fearn v Tate Gallery). Taking care is not an answer: the result for the neighbour matters.
caption: Locality, timing, sensitivity and malice tip the balance.

alt: Planning permission is not a defence, but it may change the locality. In Gillingham v Medway Dock it did, so night-time lorry noise was not a nuisance; in Wheeler v JJ Saunders pig units did not change the locality and the smell was a nuisance. Coventry v Lawrence: limited relevance to liability, possible relevance to remedy.
caption: Ask whether the permission changed the neighbourhood, not whether the activity was permitted.

after: ## Part 2: the rule in Rylands v Fletcher
alt: Five elements of Rylands v Fletcher, each with a case where it failed or was met: accumulation (Giles v Walker), something likely to do mischief (Transco), non-natural use (Rickards v Lothian; Cambridge Water), escape (Read v J Lyons) and damage of a foreseeable type (Cambridge Water). After Transco the claimant needs an interest in land and cannot recover for personal injury; Stannard v Gore shows fire cases rarely fit.
caption: All five elements are needed; most claims fail on one of them.

alt: A plan of Kemi’s repair shop, with compressors and drums of paint thinner, next to Leo’s flat, where Leo owns and Ana lodges. Noise until midnight crosses the fence and thinner seeps under it into Leo’s garden. Leo can sue in nuisance (Halsey) and under Rylands; Ana cannot sue (Hunter v Canary Wharf). Remedies: damages and an injunction limiting hours.
caption: Same facts, two torts: deal with each separately and check who can sue.
